cards.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them

depth.text: an Italian farmer planted **mystery attic seeds** and found **hardy wheat** with **seven ears**

Food scientists identified it as **poulard wheat**, and Grossi dubbed it **grano del miracolo**. It fared better during droughts and needed no fertilizer or herbicides, but heavy winds, rains and hail could make its tall stems flip over before the grain ripened.

Spelt has thicker hulls and wears down the mill faster so the mills switched to the new wheat and the farmers all had to switch too. Based on the name I think ur (ancient) Dinkel (spelt) is even older than regular…

The damage by the "progress" is multifold and pervasive. GM foods, with a goal of high yields, lost all nutritional value and gave the world insipid food and killed the natural foods forever. Supply chains and food regulations meant extreme processing of already killed food. What's left is bacteria-less, nutrition-less, sugary pulp that digests easily, increasing the consumption and economy. If I…
This is interesting for people with gluten allergies, maybe there is a way they could one day consume the ancient wheat.

It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. + It's height can be a liability. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests. + Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali, Perobelli…

Not only is this absurd ("children" need all amino acids to grow...as does anyone else), arginine isn’t even one of the essential amino acids. Your body makes it unless something is seriously wrong.

cards.title: Anthropic blocks users for anything touching training larger models

depth.text: a user says Anthropic **blocked him** for research involving **training larger models**

Jiahao Shao says the rollouts came from a **strong open-source model**, while Claude only helped submit jobs and run analysis. He says he was tagged for **“training a competitor”**; work touching RFT, SFT, or larger-model training could get him blocked, downgrade Opus 5.5 to Opus 5, or kill the session.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the rules block legitimate research and protect Anthropic’s moat; others suspect the training activity or a VPN may have triggered safeguards, and one commenter says it was an interrupted query, not a ban.

comments.text: It's very clear to me that however much you like Claude and Anthropic models, every professional user shoudl be actively cultivating a set of alternatives and fallbacks to use and seeking to ensure the overall ecosystem is as open, standardised and portable as possible. Anthropic is highly opinionated, dogmatic and idealistic. They have made a pragmatic decision already to cut loose a whole…

Something I've seen it do recently is refusing to extract services out of my own monolith code base because it finds copying code morally wrong. But its refusal to work pattern is getting pretty obnoxious. Another one I ran into last week was it refused to start a developer session to do browser testing for a code base it was working on because signing in was suddenly against it's programming. It…

Intelligence has to become a commodity. If your setup does not allow you to hot-swap a Claude Code with a Pi running astra and move on, you will be in trouble. Five years ago I was spending up to €1000 a day in Google ads for my star-map company, Greaterskies. After a few months of meetings with an ever-rotating group of "experts" working for Google, and advising me in my ads strategy, I had…

Claude’s aggressive classifier and highly opinionated rules make the recent models a giant pain to work with. It’s a great coding model but I argue with it at least once a day. It even injects its dumb rules and moral standing into artifacts it creates, like I asked a cloud session to help me create a system prompt to remove “Generated by Claude” footers from everything and the output had a…

This user is based in Hong Kong, where Claude is geo-blocked and not available. If you try visiting claude.ai from a Hong Kong IP address, you get an "unavailable in this region" message. They are likely accessing Claude via a VPN. Doing model training work over a VPN is a highly suspicious signal, and likely triggers Anthropic's classifiers. It's not surprising that their account got flagged.

cards.title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4

depth.text: Jepsen found a database **losing saved data** and **returning rows** for queries that should find none
Tests found **aborted and intermediate reads** and lost updates, even with a **single server and no faults**. Jepsen recommends **halting further deployment** and migrating to other databases.

cards.camps: Two camps: some admire the team's effort and say Jepsen's feedback could help build trust; others call the report a clown show and say they would never use its software.

comments.text: Brutal! > ParticleDB 1.1.4 claimed to be a Postgres-compatible database ... Instead, we found a library of confusion > exhibited frequent, profound transactional anomalies in essentially every way we could measure. We routinely observed the loss of committed writes, internal consistency violations, G1a (Aborted Read), G1b (Intermediate Read), and P4 (Lost Update). In the append workload…

I’ve come to learn an interesting dichotomy in software: Some software is correct by construction, in the sense that the overall design makes sense and the cases that don’t work are generally local bugs. Some software is incorrect by construction, and it tends to work by some combination of luck and by carefully working around the incorrect design in most or all code paths that could expose the…

> Given the severity and extent of the safety errors we found, and the process which produced them, Jepsen recommends users halt further deployment of ParticleDB and migrate to other databases as soon as possible. Consider checking and/or rebuilding database state from more reliable sources, if available. I guess that's what happens when you vibecode a database...

> ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.

> We present 96 issues in ParticleDB, ranging from the pedestrian (crashes, deadlocks, data loss, etc.) to the piquant (partially-invisible rows which could not be deleted, WHERE 4 = 5, dropped tables re-emerging in distorted forms, confused columns, strings turning into integers, and so on). Definitely seems worse than usual (looking back most databases seem to have <10 issues total, and the…

cards.title: It's the memory latency, stupid

depth.text: someone sped up **GROUP BY** queries by **splitting rows** into chunks that fit in **CPU caches**

**Radix partitioning** splits rows into 4096 partitions so each aggregation table is more likely to fit in cache. The second run fell from **3.6s to 2.7 seconds**, while the amount pulled from DRAM dropped from **4.5GB to 1.5GB**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some like the author's coherent explanation; others say this aggregation method is old news and ask why Pivot exists alongside DuckDB and Clickhouse.

comments.text: I work with another team at work that uses lots of message passing, C++ virtual methods in deeply nested class hierarchies, large DOMs and off-the-shelf C++ STL containers... on a STM32MP1, which has an in-order Cortex-A7 and a pittance of cache. On the other hand, in my team I wrote my custom C++ STL containers that allocate inline, SAX-style processing libraries and an object pool with links…
https://people.freebsd.org/~lstewart/articles/cpumemory.pdf Has anyone rewritten this for 2026?
I feel like the solution presented is just a clustered hashmap or “locality sensitive” if you’d like it. Still not orders of magnitude better.

Uh, isn't this just radix-partitioned aggregation? Hierarchical (fixed two level) aggregation is old. What's novel here? Microcosm of Pivot itself I guess. I just don't get why this project exists when DuckDB and Clickhouse both exist.

Shout out to the author, it seems coherent. I like flamegraphs I know folks use perf to help generate them But in the future, now that Llm is here, get and agent to check assembly, PMUs and also see what you’re doing in assembly. My 2c and happy coding to everyone :)

cards.title: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard

depth.text: someone got a **team of AI models** to solve coding problems **better** than one model alone

Memdoor rebuilt the authors' loop as a workflow where agents start with **fresh contexts** and talk only through files; a shell script, not a model, decides whether a solution passes. On the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems over five passes, Qwen3.8-27B averaged **9.8 of 10**, versus 9.6 for the authors' harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone. The **comparison is limited**: Fable 5's scores came from the authors' files, not runs in this harness, and possible training-data contamination can't be ruled out.

cards.camps: Some commenters see multi-agent setups as a promising way to lift a model's performance; others say ten problems from an old benchmark are too little to support broad claims.

comments.text: Maybe slightly off-topic from the main article but is there a good resource or site that clearly helps understand which of the "open" models are good for programming tasks, like C, C++, Python, Java? I've looked and there are tons of sites that aggregate models vs. benchmarks but I'm not sure how much of that is trust worthy.

We desperately need to keep local models competitive with the hyper scalers. I won't want to be beholden to them and their whims forever. With anthropic now restricting game reverse engineering I think we're about to cross a Rubicon of censorship.

That's pretty interesting, because with the Bonsai 2 quantisations it is quite achievable to get Qwen 27B running at 50 t/s on reasonably priced gaming machine [0]. Which in turn suggests that Fable 5 coding performance can be achieved locally with a bit of clever harnessing. Although the same harnessing should also improve Fable's performance. The important thing here is the cap for local…

There is something to say about the power of brute force approaches. Right now scaling multi agent is seemingly what is becoming the next important axis, though very strongly constrained by quality of communication protocol and compute. Even if one model is not strong enough individually, more models and more attempts as well as differing opinions may nudge the models into a better solution…

Remember those gpus into chips https://inference-docs.cerebras.ai/models/qwen-3.8-27b , where you have this chip that implements a model that run at those extremely high speeds... the ones that people ask "why do we need that"... if this is true... one of those chips with the correct harness is all that's needed to get fable like intelligence in every single computer in this planet... cards.title: GPT-5.6 Sol can beat Factorio on peaceful mode

depth.text: someone got an AI through **Factorio without biters**, though it had to **ferry supplies** by hand

**GPT-5.6 Sol** ran in Codex at low thinking level and finished the no-biter run in **13.5 hours** of game time. The rocket launch depended on **ferrying supplies** between factory areas after Sol failed to connect some production systems.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters call this an impressive benchmark for model capabilities; others say peaceful mode, game guides, and hand-fed supplies make the result less convincing.

comments.text: > The rocket launch was only achieved through significant ‘manual’ effort on Sol’s part as it papered over its late-game failures to connect certain production systems by repeatedly ferrying supplies between areas of the factory. Robots: they're just like us!

If you haven't been keeping an eye on LLMs playing games, GPT 6.1 Sol can new beat games 100% vision-only (without harnesses that give the agent extra information about the game). Pokemon is no longer a difficult challenge for it, even with additional difficulty restrictions such as hard mode and level caps. Recently, GPT 6.1 Sol beat Final Fantasy VII and its bonus bosses vision-only…
Watching AI play games is fun, but I can't wait for someone to crack having small LLMs in games to enrich them in useful and interesting ways.

One limitation of these type of demos (and similar with Minecraft, etc) is that:
1. Putting into "peaceful" mode makes response time a non-factor
2. These models have read and have access to every guide and video ever published on the subject. Most humans, especially on first play, learn game systems and interactions from scratch, then develop novel strategies and plans and "hypothesis test"…

It doesn't seem to understand the core mechanic of Factorio, which is putting outputs onto belts and routing them to other inputs. It does this in a few places, but for the most part everything is put into chests and moved around by the player.

glossary.poulard wheat: A kind of wheat; food scientists identified Grossi’s grain by this name.
glossary.herbicides: Chemicals used to kill unwanted plants, such as weeds.
glossary.leaven: To make dough rise before baking.
glossary.gluten: A group of proteins in wheat that helps dough stretch and hold together.
glossary.heritage grains: Older kinds of grain kept and grown from earlier farming traditions.
glossary.RFT: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning: a way to improve an AI by rewarding stronger answers to practice tasks.
glossary.SFT: Supervised fine-tuning: training a model on examples of desired answers.
glossary.distilled: Used one AI’s answers as examples to train another AI.
glossary.rollouts: The attempts and results a model produces while working through a task, which can be used as training examples.
glossary.open-source model: An AI model whose underlying pieces are made available for others to use or build on.
glossary.G1a (Aborted Read): A read that sees a change from a database transaction that later failed.
glossary.G1b (Intermediate Read): A read that sees a temporary change before the transaction that made it is finished.
glossary.P4 (Lost Update): When one saved change overwrites another, so the earlier change disappears.
glossary.WAL: Write-ahead log: a record of changes the database saves so it can recover or copy them.
glossary.TLA+: Temporal Logic of Actions: a language for describing how a system can change over time so you can check whether it follows rules.
glossary.GROUP BY: A database operation that puts rows with the same value together and calculates something for each group.
glossary.CPU cache: A small, fast storage area in a processor that keeps data handy so it can be used quickly.
glossary.radix partitioning: A way to split data into groups first, then process each smaller group separately.
glossary.HashMap: A way for a program to look up a value using a key, like finding a count for each UserID.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory: the working memory a computer uses while running things.
glossary.mechanical sympathy: Writing software with an eye to how the computer's hardware actually works.
glossary.multi-agent: A setup where several AI workers each handle a role and work toward one result.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.hidden tests: Checks kept secret from the builder, used to see whether the finished program works.
glossary.contamination: When a model has already seen test problems during training, so a score may not show how well it handles new problems.
glossary.peaceful mode: A game setting that removes the biters, the hostile bugs mentioned in the comments.
glossary.transport belt: A conveyor in the game that carries items between parts of a factory.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
